To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

asbestos bodies are of value in ascribing unusual exposures only when present in large numbers, that the mean number of fibers in lungs from the general population is 1 x 10(6), and that the grade of asbestos is closely related to the total number of fibers present.

asbestos bodies are of little diagnostic value in ascertained asbestos exposure; that numbers of asbestos fibers in the lung are not related to ascertained asbestos fiber exposure; that total numbers of fibers are not related to disease severity; that numbers of fibers in the lung of a patient with mesothelioma may be much smaller than those in a patient with asbestosis; that numbers of long thin amphiboles are closely related to disease; and that numbers of fibers less than 5 mu m in length
asbestos-related disease in the lung is not merely a function of the total numbers of fibers, but that factors related to fiber type and fiber size are also important.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and quantitation of asbestos fibers and asbestos bodies in lung tissue and the relationship of the findings to the pathogenesis of the disease.
the identification of the types of fibers in lung tissue, the numbers of fibers present (total and by type), and the distribution of fibers in lung.
the identification of asbestos fibers in human lung, with the analysis of fiber burdens in various types of asbestos-related disease, and with the development of techniques for fiber analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the number of fibers present in lungs of patients with asbestos-related disease is greater than the number in lungs of persons from the general population; that the numbers of asbestos bodies present in lung are not useful in determining the relationship of a particular lesion to asbestos exposure; that the numbers and types of fibers in lungs of patients are closely related to the type of disease present; and that the numbers and sizes of asbestos fibers are related to the severity of disease.
the presence of long amphibole fibers in a given lesion indicates a relationship to asbestos exposure, whereas the absence of such fibers indicates no relationship to asbestos exposure.
asbestos-related disease can only be attributed to asbestos exposure on a case-by-case basis by analysis of numbers and types and sizes of fibers in lung.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
asbestos-related diseases occur only after prolonged exposure to long thin fibers.
the fiber type and size, not the total fiber number, is most important.
the number and types of fibers in the lung are closely related to the type and severity of asbestos-related disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fiber burden in the lungs is not related to the severity of the disease.
the number of fibers present is not the only factor that determines the development of disease.
fiber counting is a valuable tool in the diagnosis of the asbestos-related diseases.
